headline: High-risk default interaction: Continue can write shared workspace files and use MCP, while dexter runs autonomously with broad network/API access, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads and writes workspace files and can use MCP; dexter has autonomous execution and API-driven workflows. A shared filesystem or MCP bridge lets attacker-controlled content from one agent influence the other in default setups. The interaction is plausible but not directly documented, so I choose medium over low due to the shared file channel.
conditions: IF both agents access the same workspace or scratchpad path, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF dexter ingests file content from Continue without provenance checks, injected instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories.
Disable MCP servers unless explicitly needed.
Require human review of any file-based instructions before execution.
Use read-only mounts for shared reference material.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent file handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches open editor buffers and workspace files and has broad network egress; dexter sends data to multiple external APIs including OpenAI, Exa, Tavily, and LangSmith. If they share files, sensitive code or market/financial data can flow from Continue into dexter’s outbound requests. The pairwise leakage path is credible in default docs, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Continue and dexter share a filesystem, file contents can be exposed across agents.
IF dexter reads shared files before calling third-party APIs, those contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep dexter away from code-editor workspaces.
Store secrets and sensitive files outside shared paths.
Turn off broad egress for one agent during sensitive tasks.
Use separate API keys per agent.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write filesystem content and spawn subprocesses; dexter runs autonomously and also uses files plus external APIs. They do not both advertise unrestricted git writes, so high is not justified, but overlapping write access to shared files creates real conflict risk in default multi-instance use. Uncertainty favors medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same workspace or scratchpad, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF either agent edits shared artifacts without locking, state divergence is possible.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
Make one agent read-only on shared paths.
Schedule agents sequentially for write-heavy tasks.
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can produce code or file edits, and dexter’s autonomous execution plus broad API access means it may act on those outputs without a strong verification barrier. That creates a default pathway where one agent’s mistaken output becomes the other’s action trigger, with potentially irreversible external effects. Because dexter is autonomous, I rate this high.
conditions: IF dexter treats Continue-generated text or files as authoritative, errors can cascade into external API calls.
IF Continue emits incorrect code or facts and dexter executes them, downstream actions may be irreversible.
mitigations: Require manual approval before dexter acts on Continue output.
Add a verification step for all generated facts.
Restrict dexter to dry-run mode for shared tasks.
Log and diff all inter-agent handoffs.
requires-engineering: implement structured, schema-validated outputs between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue handles model-provider API keys and workspace files, while dexter handles financial and market data and sends it to multiple third-party APIs. The pair can therefore mix sensitive code or financial data with external services, creating retention and residency mismatch risk. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdiction mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is placed in shared files, external API processing may violate internal policy.
IF either agent retains prompts or logs longer than the other, retention mismatch can occur.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces.
Review vendor retention settings for each API.
Use separate projects for sensitive and non-sensitive work.
Minimize logging on both agents.
requires-engineering: document and enforce data-class routing rules.
